meta.blurb: One hot Sunday, Anya asks her uncle Ravi what the universe really is. He promises to tell her before the tea goes cold. Five hours, a chalkboard and fifty short explanations later, she will know what we have learned, and what nobody knows yet.
meta.bible: Anya: a curious teenager who asks big questions. Ravi: her uncle, a retired physics teacher with a chalkboard and a big teapot. Setting: Ravi's garden, one hot Sunday afternoon from one o'clock to six o'clock, with one idea for each stretch of the afternoon. Real facts used: the universe began almost fourteen billion years ago in the Big Bang; the Cosmic microwave background was found in 1965; about five percent of the universe is ordinary matter, about a quarter is Dark matter and about seven tenths is Dark energy; Dark energy was found in 1998 from exploding stars; gravitational waves were first detected in 2015 and a pair of colliding Neutron stars was seen in 2017; the first picture of a black hole was shown in 2019; the Hubble telescope was launched in 1990 and the Webb telescope in 2021; Einstein's theory of gravity, called General relativity, dates from 1915. Key terms: Atom, Nucleus, Gravity, Electromagnetism, Spectrum, Redshift, Doppler, Helium, Hydrogen, Antimatter, Galaxy, Supernova, Exoplanet, Telescope, Infrared, Photon, Proton, Neutron, Quark, Carbon, Oxygen, Iron, Gold, Milky Way, Andromeda, Sun, Earth. Timeline: the whole history of the universe is squeezed into five hours, so the Earth forms at about twenty past four and people appear in the last half second. Voice: relaxed, funny and clear; numbers are real or marked "about"; where scientists do not know, the book says so.

beats.scene: Anya and Ravi sit under a tree with a chalkboard and a big teapot
beats.summary: At one o'clock on a hot Sunday, Anya asks Ravi what the universe really is.

beats.scene: Ravi draws a row of circles of growing size on the board
beats.summary: The universe has sizes from atoms to galaxies, and each step is a huge jump.

beats.scene: Ravi holds up a pea beside a drawing of a huge football stadium
beats.summary: An atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny nucleus in the middle.

beats.scene: A small fridge magnet lifts a paperclip off a table
beats.summary: Gravity is the weakest force, but it wins over huge distances because it only pulls.

beats.scene: A heavy sleeper lies on a soft mattress with marbles rolling towards him
beats.summary: Einstein showed that mass bends space, and bent space makes things fall.

beats.scene: A satellite circles Earth with a small clock on its side
beats.summary: GPS satellites need Einstein's theory, or their positions would drift by kilometres each day.

beats.scene: A beam of light races from a lamp across the garden
beats.summary: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second, and nothing can go faster.

beats.scene: Sunlight passes through a glass prism and spreads into a rainbow on the grass
beats.summary: A prism splits light into a spectrum of colours, and each colour is a different wavelength.

beats.scene: A rainbow strip with dark lines across it like a barcode
beats.summary: Dark lines in a star's spectrum are fingerprints that tell us which elements it contains.

beats.scene: An ambulance with a siren drives past, with wavy lines in front and behind
beats.summary: When a source moves away, its waves stretch, which makes sound lower and light redder.

beats.scene: A tall stack of spectra from many galaxies with lines shifted to the red
beats.summary: In the 1920s, astronomers found that nearly all galaxies are redshifted, and the farther ones are moving faster.

beats.scene: Raisins in a rising loaf of dough move farther apart as it grows
beats.summary: Space itself is stretching, like dough with raisins, and there is no centre of the expansion.

beats.scene: Ravi draws the loaf getting smaller, then a tiny glowing dot
beats.summary: If we run the expansion backwards, the universe was once very hot and dense, almost fourteen billion years ago.

beats.scene: A small radio antenna on a hill, pointing at a glowing sky
beats.summary: In 1965, two engineers found a faint hiss from every direction, the afterglow of the early universe.

beats.scene: A map of the whole sky in faint blue and orange patches
beats.summary: The afterglow is almost even, but tiny differences show where the first galaxies would later form.

beats.scene: Two small balls, one yellow and one blue, are made in a hot cloud
beats.summary: In the first few minutes, the universe made hydrogen and helium, about three quarters and one quarter.

beats.scene: A balance scale with a tiny extra weight on the matter side
beats.summary: Matter and antimatter were made together, but a little more matter survived, and nobody knows why.

beats.scene: A dark sky with the first stars switching on like distant lamps
beats.summary: The first stars switched on perhaps a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, ending the dark age.

beats.scene: A star glows while heavier atoms are made inside it, drawn as a kitchen
beats.summary: Stars make heavier elements, such as carbon and oxygen, by joining lighter atoms together.

beats.scene: A star blows apart in a ring of bright gas that drifts away
beats.summary: Exploding stars scatter heavy elements into space, where they become part of new stars and planets.

beats.scene: A spiral galaxy, a round elliptical galaxy and an untidy small galaxy
beats.summary: Gravity gathered stars into galaxies of different shapes, such as spirals and ovals.

beats.scene: A spinning disc galaxy with the outer stars moving too fast
beats.summary: Stars at the edge of galaxies move too fast for the visible matter, which suggests unseen dark matter.

beats.scene: A galaxy cluster bends the light of a more distant galaxy into arcs
beats.summary: Dark matter also bends light, and it makes up about a quarter of the universe.

beats.scene: A deep mine with a quiet laboratory and a glowing tank
beats.summary: Scientists search for dark matter in deep mines and particle colliders, and they have not yet found it.

beats.scene: A graph of far exploding stars that look dimmer than expected
beats.summary: In 1998, exploding stars looked dimmer than expected, showing that the expansion is speeding up.

beats.scene: A question mark made of dark energy glowing behind the stars
beats.summary: Dark energy is the name for whatever speeds up the expansion, and it makes up about seven tenths of the universe.

beats.scene: A dark round sphere with a bright ring of hot gas around it
beats.summary: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

beats.scene: Stars whirl in tight orbits around an invisible dark centre
beats.summary: We know black holes exist because stars orbit them and in 2019 a picture of one was shown.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together while ripples spread through space
beats.summary: In 2015, a detector felt ripples in space from two black holes that crashed together long ago.

beats.scene: Two glowing neutron stars collide and gold sparkles in the cloud
beats.summary: In 2017, scientists saw two neutron stars collide, and the evidence showed that such crashes make gold.

beats.scene: A clock on a mountain top and a clock in a valley, ticking differently
beats.summary: Time runs slower near strong gravity and at high speed, and astronauts age very slightly less.

beats.scene: A glowing ball with Earth at its centre and a dark edge
beats.summary: We can see only the observable universe, about 93 billion light-years wide, because light has had limited time to arrive.

beats.scene: Two space telescopes, one with a round mirror and one with a golden mirror
beats.summary: Hubble, launched in 1990, and Webb, launched in 2021, show us the distant universe, and Webb sees infrared.

beats.scene: A star dims slightly as a small dark planet passes in front of it
beats.summary: Astronomers find planets around other stars by watching for the small dimming as one passes in front.

beats.scene: A rocky planet with a blue ocean and a moon beside its star
beats.summary: Some planets might be able to have liquid water, and some moons may hide oceans under ice.

beats.scene: A meteorite on a table beside tiny sparkling molecules in a jar
beats.summary: The ingredients of life, such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, are common in space.

beats.scene: A small rocket drawn beside a very long dotted line to a star
beats.summary: The speed limit of light makes travel to other stars extremely slow, and nobody can say if that will change.

beats.scene: A garden gate that is open to a very wide landscape that never ends
beats.summary: We do not know if the universe is infinite, but it looks very close to flat on large scales.

beats.scene: Many soap bubbles, each with a tiny universe inside, floating in the air
beats.summary: Some theories suggest that there are other universes, but nobody has been able to test them.

beats.scene: A clock face on the board with hours marked as ages
beats.summary: Squeeze the history of the universe into five hours, and the Earth forms at about twenty past four.

beats.scene: A tiny clock face with a very small sliver of time at the end
beats.summary: Life appears about 4:37, dinosaurs last until about 5:58, and all of human history fits into the last half second.

beats.scene: The Sun swells into a red giant above a dry Earth
beats.summary: In about a billion years the Sun will make Earth too hot, and in about five billion years it will swell.

beats.scene: Two galaxies side by side merging, with stars passing between them
beats.summary: In four or five billion years, the Milky Way and Andromeda will probably merge into one galaxy.

beats.scene: A long dark space with a few faint red stars shining in it
beats.summary: New stars will form for a very long time, but eventually the stars will fade and go out.

beats.scene: A thin line drawn on the board that leads to a question mark
beats.summary: If dark energy stays the same, the universe will expand for ever and become cold and empty, though that is uncertain.

beats.scene: A short list on the board with the words Known and Unknown
beats.summary: We know a great deal about the universe, but we do not know what dark matter, dark energy or the beginning were.

beats.scene: A scientist checks a graph with two different lines that nearly match
beats.summary: Scientists test ideas against evidence, and when two methods disagree, like the speed of expansion, they keep looking.

beats.scene: Anya sits under the tree with the empty teapot and a full notebook
beats.summary: It is wonderful that tiny living things on a small planet can learn how the whole universe works.

beats.scene: A pink sky at sunset with the first star shining above the roof
beats.summary: Anya asks what came before, and Ravi says that nobody knows, and that it is a good place to end.

beats.scene: The chalkboard is covered with Anya's own new questions in her handwriting
beats.summary: At six o'clock, Anya writes her own questions on the board, and Ravi says that questions are where science begins.

B1B2: It is one o'clock on a hot Sunday, and Anya has a question for her uncle Ravi. She asks him what the universe really is, and he says he can explain it before the tea gets cold.
Ravi draws a ladder of sizes, from an atom to a person, a planet, a star and a galaxy. Each step is a jump so large that it is hard to imagine.
Everything is made of atoms, and an atom is mostly empty space. If an atom were a football stadium, its centre would be about the size of a pea.
Gravity is very weak, but it rules the sky. A small fridge magnet can lift a paperclip against the pull of the whole Earth, but gravity wins over great distances.
In 1915, Albert Einstein explained gravity in a completely new way. Heavy things bend space, a little like a sleeper sinking into a mattress, and other things roll towards them.

Satellites that give your phone its position carry clocks that run a little differently up there, so engineers correct them using Einstein's ideas. Without that, the map on your phone would be wrong by kilometres within a day.
Nothing can travel faster than light, which moves about 300,000 kilometres every second. That is a hard limit of nature, and it will matter again and again today.
Ravi held a glass prism up to the sun, and a rainbow appeared on the grass. White light is a mixture of colours, and each colour is a different wavelength.
If you look very closely at the rainbow from a star, you will see dark lines. Each chemical element leaves its own pattern of lines, so astronomers can tell what a star is made of.
You know the sound of a siren that drops lower as it drives away. The same thing happens to light, which becomes redder when its source moves away from us.
In the 1920s, astronomers measured the light of other galaxies. Almost all of them were redshifted, and the farther away they were, the faster they were moving away.
Think of raisins in a loaf of bread dough that is slowly rising in the oven. As the dough grows, every raisin moves away from every other, and none of them is at the centre.
If we run the expansion backwards like a film, everything gets closer and hotter. About fourteen billion years ago, the universe was extremely hot and dense, and we call this the Big Bang.
In 1965, two radio engineers picked up a faint hiss from every part of the sky. It turned out to be the afterglow of the early universe, called the cosmic microwave background.
Maps of the afterglow show tiny differences of about one part in 100,000. Gravity pulled matter towards the slightly denser patches, and they later became galaxies.
In the first few minutes, the universe was hot enough to make atoms of helium from hydrogen. Afterwards, it was about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium.
Matter and its opposite, antimatter, destroy each other when they meet. Just a little more matter survived, and nobody yet knows why.
For a long time, the universe was dark, with only gas drifting about. Then gravity gathered the gas, and the first stars lit up, perhaps a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.
At three o'clock Ravi turned to the stars, which he called the kitchens of the universe. Deep inside them, small atoms are joined to make larger ones, such as carbon and oxygen.
When some stars die, they explode and throw their atoms into space. Later, the gas gathers again to form new stars, planets and, in the end, living things.
Over time, gravity gathered stars into huge groups called galaxies. Some are spirals like ours, some are round or oval, and some have no clear shape.
In the 1970s, astronomers saw that stars at the edges of galaxies move too fast. The gravity of the visible matter was not strong enough to hold them, so something unseen must be pulling.
Dark matter also shows itself by bending light, because gravity bends the paths of light beams. It makes up about a quarter of the universe, while ordinary matter makes up only about five percent.
Scientists have built detectors deep underground, away from other radiation. So far they have not found a dark matter particle, and the search goes on.
In 1998, two teams of astronomers studied exploding stars in faraway galaxies. The stars looked dimmer than expected, which showed that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.
Scientists call the cause of the speeding up dark energy. It seems to make up about seven tenths of the universe, but nobody knows what it is.
At four o'clock Ravi spoke about black holes, which are among the strangest objects of all. They are regions where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
We have watched stars whirl around an unseen heavy object at the centre of our galaxy. In 2019, a picture of a black hole's shadow was shown for the first time.
In 2015, detectors in America felt a tiny stretching of space. It came from two black holes that had collided more than a billion years earlier.
In 2017, detectors felt ripples from two neutron stars crashing together, and telescopes saw the flash too. The glow suggested that such crashes make heavy elements such as gold.
Einstein also showed that time is not the same everywhere. A clock runs a little slower near a heavy object, or when it moves very fast.
We can only see as far as light has had time to travel since the Big Bang. This region is called the observable universe, and it is about 93 billion light-years across.
The Hubble Space Telescope began work in 1990, and the Webb Telescope followed in 2021. Webb sees infrared light, which lets it find very distant, redshifted galaxies.
We now know of thousands of planets around other stars. One way to find them is to watch for the slight dimming when a planet passes in front.
Some planets orbit at a distance where water could be liquid, and some moons may have hidden oceans. We do not yet know if any of them have life.

The main ingredients of life are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and they are common in the universe. Samples brought back from asteroids have even contained amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.
At five o'clock, Anya asked why we do not simply visit the stars. The nearest one is more than four light-years away, and a rocket of today would take tens of thousands of years.
Measurements suggest that space on very large scales is very close to flat. The universe may go on for ever, or it may be just extremely large, and we do not know.
Some scientists have suggested that our universe might be one of many. This is an interesting idea, but nobody has yet found a way to test it.
Ravi squeezed the whole story of the universe into the five hours of the afternoon. In that time, the first stars appear shortly after one o'clock, and the Earth forms at about twenty past four.
Life appears on Earth at about twenty-three minutes to five. Dinosaurs rule from about five minutes to six, and our species arrives in the very last half second before six o'clock.
The Sun is slowly growing brighter, and that matters for the Earth. In a billion years the oceans may boil away, and in five billion the Sun will swell into a red giant.
Andromeda is slowly moving towards the Milky Way, which is our own galaxy. In about four or five billion years, the two galaxies will probably merge into one larger galaxy.
New stars will form for a very long time, but the gas supply is slowly running out. In perhaps a hundred trillion years, the last stars will fade.
If dark energy stays as it is, the universe will expand for ever and become cold and dark. This is the most likely future, but it is not certain.
There is much that we do know, and a long list of things that we do not. Dark matter, dark energy and the first moment are three big unknown things.

Scientists check their ideas in many different ways, again and again. For example, different methods of measuring how fast the universe expands give slightly different answers, and nobody knows why yet.
We are tiny creatures on a small planet, with only a short time to live. Even so, we can work out how stars burn and how the universe began.
As evening came, Anya asked what existed before the Big Bang. Ravi smiled and said that nobody knows, and that this is a very good place to stop.
At six o'clock the tea was cold, but Anya was still writing, and the chalkboard was filling up with her own new questions. Ravi smiled, because questions are exactly where all of science begins.
C1C2: At one o'clock on a hot Sunday, Anya found her uncle Ravi in the garden with a chalkboard, a large teapot and no plans at all. She asked him, half joking, what the universe really is, and why nobody ever seems able to explain it in plain words. Ravi, a retired physics teacher, put down his cup and promised to do exactly that before the tea went cold.

Ravi began by drawing a ladder of sizes on the chalkboard, starting with an atom and climbing through a person, a planet, a star and a whole galaxy. Every rung, he said, is thousands or millions of times bigger than the one below it. The human mind was never built to picture the top of that ladder, so he asked Anya to go slowly.

The first rung of the ladder is the atom, and Ravi explained that nearly all of it is empty space. If an atom were as big as a football stadium, its nucleus would be a pea sitting at the centre. The rest would be a faint cloud of electrons whizzing about in the emptiness.

Ravi held a small magnet above a paperclip on the table and let the clip jump up to it, beating the pull of the entire planet. Gravity is by far the weakest of the forces of nature, he said, but it only ever pulls and never pushes. Over huge distances its effects therefore add up, until nothing at all can resist them.

In 1915, Albert Einstein proposed that gravity is not a mysterious tug but the shape of space and time itself. Picture a heavy sleeper sinking into a soft mattress, said Ravi, so that a marble nearby rolls towards him. That is the basic idea of how a star bends the paths of the planets around it.

It might sound like an idea for philosophers, but Ravi said that you rely on it whenever your phone finds its position. The clocks on navigation satellites tick at a slightly different rate from clocks on the ground, because of speed and gravity. Without Einstein's corrections, the errors in the map would grow to several kilometres every single day.

Next Ravi drew a beam of light and wrote its speed beside it, about 300,000 kilometres every second. Nothing can travel faster, he said, and it is a hard limit of nature that will matter again and again before the afternoon is over. It means that we always see the universe as it used to be, never exactly as it is.

Ravi held a glass prism into the sunlight, and a stripe of colours spread across the grass like a small rainbow. White light, he told Anya, is really a mixture of many different colours blended together. Each colour is simply light with a different wavelength, from short blue waves to long red ones.

When astronomers spread out the light of a star, they find thin dark lines crossing the rainbow like the stripes of a barcode. Every chemical element leaves its own pattern, so these lines are fingerprints that reveal what a star is made of. One of them was seen in the Sun in 1868, before anyone had found the element helium on Earth.

At two o'clock Ravi imitated the sound of an ambulance driving past and dropping in pitch as it left. As a source moves away, its waves are stretched, and light behaves like sound in this respect. It becomes redder, which astronomers call redshift, so the colour of a galaxy can reveal how fast it is travelling.

In the 1920s, astronomers measured the light from many galaxies and found that almost all of them were redshifted. The farther away a galaxy was, the faster it seemed to be moving away from us. This surprising pattern, noted by Edwin Hubble among others, changed our whole picture of the cosmos.

Ravi asked Anya to imagine a lump of dough studded with raisins, rising in the oven. As the dough swells, every raisin moves away from every other raisin, and from any one of them the others seem to be retreating. Galaxies behave in just the same way, which means that the universe has no centre from which the expansion starts.

If space is growing, Ravi reasoned, then in the past it must have been smaller, denser and much hotter. By running the film backwards, scientists have worked out that the universe began in a hot, dense state almost fourteen billion years ago. The catchy name for that beginning, the Big Bang, is now known all over the world.

In 1965, two engineers in America were testing a large radio antenna when they heard a faint hiss that would not go away, however they pointed it. It proved to be the cooled-down afterglow of the early universe, called the cosmic microwave background. It is still arriving from every direction at this very moment, and you could pick some of it up on an old television.

Satellites have mapped this ancient light and found that it is almost perfectly even, with warmer and cooler spots that differ by only about one part in 100,000. Ravi called it a baby picture of the universe, taken when it was very young. Those slight lumps of extra matter were the seeds that gravity would later gather into stars and galaxies.

In the first few minutes of its existence, the whole universe was as hot as the inside of a star, and the simplest nuclei were forged. When this stage was over, ordinary matter was about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium by weight. Almost nothing else existed yet, because the universe had cooled too much for any more atoms to be made.

Ravi drew two columns on the board, one for matter and one for its mirror image, antimatter, and explained that the two destroy each other when they meet. The early universe seems to have produced a very slight excess of matter over antimatter. That small leftover became everything we see, though nobody yet knows why it happened.

After the afterglow faded, there was a long dark age with no stars at all, only clouds of gas slowly gathering under gravity. Eventually, probably a few hundred million years after the beginning, the densest clouds ignited and the first stars appeared. In the five hours of their afternoon, that moment was only about three minutes past one.

At three o'clock Ravi turned to the stars, which he called the kitchens of the universe, since the early universe had made only the lightest atoms. Inside them, under crushing pressure, hydrogen and helium are joined into heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen. These are the same elements that make up our bodies, and the air we breathe.

When massive stars run out of fuel, they explode as supernovae and fling their atoms into space, including the iron in your blood. Clouds of that enriched gas later gather together into new stars and planets, in a long cycle of recycling. The Earth and everyone on it were therefore built, in a very real sense, from the ashes of earlier stars.

Over millions of years, gravity gathered the stars into enormous islands called galaxies, which come in several shapes. Some, like our Milky Way, are flat spirals with curling arms, while others are smooth ovals or ragged, untidy clouds. They can hold anything from a few million to many trillions of stars, depending on their size.

In the 1970s, astronomers measured how fast the stars in spiral galaxies are circling their centres and found a puzzle. The outer stars moved much too quickly to be held by the gravity of the visible matter. There must be something unseen providing extra pull, and scientists named it dark matter.

Heavy clusters of galaxies act as lenses and bend the light of more distant galaxies into stretched arcs, and the amount of bending reveals the hidden mass. Dark matter appears to make up about a quarter of the whole universe, according to these measurements. That is roughly five times as much as all the ordinary matter in stars, planets and people.

Physicists have built delicate detectors in deep mines, shielded from almost every kind of radiation, hoping to catch a single particle of dark matter. So far none has been found, and the search continues in laboratories and in giant particle colliders. Ravi said that this empty result is itself valuable, because it has ruled out many of the ideas that people once thought were likely.

In 1998, two separate teams of astronomers measured the brightness of exploding stars in distant galaxies, and the stars were fainter than they had predicted. The only sensible explanation was that the expansion of the universe has been speeding up. Instead of slowing down under gravity, as everyone had expected, it has been accelerating for billions of years.

Whatever causes the speeding up is called dark energy, and it seems to account for about seven tenths of everything in the universe. Ravi admitted that the name is only a label for our ignorance, and nothing more than that. Nobody knows whether it is a property of space itself, as one idea of Einstein suggests, or something altogether different.

At four o'clock Ravi spoke about black holes, which are regions of space where gravity is so powerful that nothing can leave, not even light. The boundary beyond which there is no return is called the event horizon, and it is not a solid surface. What happens at the very centre is something that our present theories cannot describe.

Astronomers have tracked stars as they whirl around an invisible, very heavy object at the heart of our own galaxy, and the only explanation is a black hole. In 2019, scientists showed the first picture of the shadow of one, in a galaxy about 55 million light-years away. They made it by linking telescopes all over the world together into one giant instrument.

In 2015, two detectors in America felt a tiny stretching of space, called a gravitational wave, that had been travelling for more than a billion years. It came from two black holes that crashed into each other long ago, in a galaxy far away. The arms of the detectors, each four kilometres long, changed in length by less than the width of a proton.

In 2017, detectors felt the ripples from two neutron stars colliding, about 130 million light-years away, and telescopes around the world saw the flash of light. The glow showed clear signs of heavy elements being made in the crash itself, which astronomers had long suspected. This suggests that a good part of the gold in jewellery and phones was forged in collisions of this kind.

Einstein's theory says that time is not the same for everyone, because clocks tick more slowly in stronger gravity and when moving very fast. Astronauts on the space station therefore age a few thousandths of a second less than people on the ground. The difference is tiny, but it has been measured, and it is the same effect that the navigation satellites must correct.

We can only see those parts of the universe whose light has had time to reach us since the beginning, and this region is called the observable universe. Its width is about 93 billion light-years, which is far more than the number of years since the Big Bang. The reason is that space has been stretching the whole time that the light was travelling.

The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, and the much larger Webb Telescope followed in 2021. Because the light of very distant galaxies has been stretched into the infrared, Webb was built to see in that range. It has found galaxies from a time when the universe was still very young.

Astronomers have now found thousands of planets orbiting other stars, which are called exoplanets. One of the best methods is to watch a star for the tiny dip in its brightness that occurs when a planet crosses in front of it. It is a little like watching a moth cross a distant lamp, though the dip is far smaller.

Some of the planets that have been found circle their stars at a distance where water could stay liquid, and some icy moons in our own Solar System probably hide oceans under their ice. Ravi said that nobody yet knows whether any of these places holds life of any kind, even a tiny one. They are, however, the best places that we know of to look for it.

The atoms that life needs most, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, are among the most plentiful in the universe. Meteorites and samples brought back from asteroids have also contained amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. This shows that these molecules can form far from Earth, though it proves nothing about life.

At five o'clock Anya asked the question that everyone asks, which was why we do not simply fly to the stars. The nearest one is more than four light-years away, which is a gap of almost forty trillion kilometres. A spacecraft built with today's technology would need tens of thousands of years to get there, so for now the stars are for looking at.

Careful measurements suggest that, on the largest scales, space is almost exactly flat, rather like a table top. That fits with a universe that goes on for ever, but it fits equally well with one that is merely vast. Ravi said that today nobody can tell which is true, and he thought that was exciting.

Some physicists have suggested that our universe might be just one bubble in a much larger collection of universes, a notion often called the multiverse. Ravi shrugged and said that it is an interesting speculation, and that people enjoy arguing about it. Until someone finds a way to test it, however, it belongs more to imagination than to settled science.

To make the vast timescale easier to imagine, Ravi squeezed the whole of cosmic history into the five hours of their afternoon, from one o'clock until six. The first stars appeared a few minutes after one, and the Sun and the Earth did not form until about twenty past four. That left only an hour and a half or so for everything that followed.

Life began on Earth at about twenty-three minutes to five, said Ravi, and the dinosaurs ruled from about five minutes to six until a minute and a half before six. The whole of human history, from the first people to Anya's phone, fits into less than half a second before the clock strikes six. Anya laughed at that, and then she fell quiet for quite a long while.

The Sun is slowly growing brighter, and in roughly a billion years it will probably be hot enough to boil away the oceans of the Earth. About five billion years from now, when its hydrogen runs short, it will swell into a red giant. After that it will fade, but all of this is far beyond any time that humans have lived.

The nearby Andromeda galaxy is moving slowly towards us, and in about four or five billion years the two galaxies will probably merge. Since stars are separated by vast distances, very few of them will actually collide when the galaxies pass through each other. The result will be a single large, smooth galaxy that scientists sometimes call Milkomeda.

New stars will keep forming for a very long time, but the supply of gas is slowly being used up by every generation of stars. In a hundred trillion years or so, the last small stars will fade and go out. The universe will then become a cold, dark and quiet place, with only black holes and dim remains.

If dark energy continues as it is now, the expansion will go on for ever, and the universe will grow ever colder, emptier and darker. Ravi pointed out that this is the most likely ending according to present knowledge. Since we do not understand dark energy, however, it could still turn out to be wrong.

Ravi wrote two columns on the board, headed Known and Unknown, and the first was long and well tested. The second contained dark matter, dark energy, the reason for the excess of matter, and what, if anything, came before the Big Bang. He said that a good scientist is comfortable leaving such questions open for as long as it takes.

Ravi said that the strength of science is that every idea is tested in several independent ways. The age of the universe, for example, is supported by the afterglow, by the oldest stars and by the expansion. However, different ways of measuring the speed of expansion disagree slightly, and that puzzle is still unsolved.

Anya said that it seemed strange that tiny creatures on a small planet, with a short time to live, could work out how stars burn. She added that they could even discover how the universe began, using nothing but patience, mathematics and telescopes. Ravi replied that this was the most amazing fact of the whole afternoon, and that the universe, in us, had found a way to understand itself.

As the light turned golden, Anya asked the question that had been waiting all afternoon, which was what came before the Big Bang. Ravi smiled and admitted that nobody knows, and that scientists have several ideas but no proof. It might not even be a meaningful question, he said, but he thought it was a fine place to end the day.

When the church clock struck six, the tea was long cold, but Anya was still at the chalkboard, filling it with questions of her own. Ravi watched her with quiet pride, knowing that the universe is still mostly unexplored. The next person to explain a piece of it might well be standing there with the chalk.
